name: Washington Square Park
short_description: Iconic Greenwich Village landmark and NYU social center; one of NYC's most-visited public squares with the Stanford White marble arch. Very high tourist gravity.

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Iconic Greenwich Village landmark and NYU social center; one of NYC's most-visited public squares with the Stanford White marble arch. Very high tourist gravity.

beats.script_body: Greenwich Village started as its own village — a place where, as in Boccaccio's Decameron, the well-to-do fled on a near-yearly basis to escape the plagues of colonial Nieuw Amsterdam and then New York City, mostly recurrent bouts of yellow fever. Building began in earnest in the 1820s and 1830s, with wealthy families putting up row house after row house in what was then a suburb. Then the city caught up: the hoi polloi moved in just down the block, and the bluebloods did the 19th-century version of urban flight, decamping a mile uptown. Their swank houses were carved into cheap apartments and boarding houses, or torn down for factories, and the neighborhood filled with immigrants and, later, artists. It kept its status as a place apart thanks to its tangle of twisting, narrow streets — "The streets have run crazy and broken themselves," O. Henry wrote, "into strange angles and curves. One street crosses itself a time or two." In the 1960s and '70s that quiet charm drew the wealthy back, and it became a hideaway once more.

beats.source_passage: Greenwich Village started as its own village, a place where, as in Boccaccio's Decameron, the well-to-do fled on a near-yearly basis to escape the plagues of colonial Nieuw Amsterdam and then New York City (recurrent bouts of yellow fever, mostly). Building began in earnest in the 1820s and 1830s, with wealthy families building row house after row house in what was then a suburb. Soon, of course, the city caught up, the hoi polloi were living just down the block, and the bluebloods did the 19th-century version of urban flight and moved a mile uptown to newer suburbs. Their swank houses were subdivided into cheap apartments and boarding houses, or torn down entirely to create factories. The neighborhood became home to immigrants and later, artists. The Village always retained its status as a place apart, however, thanks to the confusing configuration of its streets, a jumble of twisting byways and narrow streets. "The streets have run crazy and broken themselves . . . into strange angles and curves," O. Henry wrote. "One street crosses itself a time or two." In the 1960s and '70s, the charm of this urban topography, the quiet of the tiny streets cut off from upper Manhattan's bustle, brought the well-to-do back, and the neighborhood became once more a hideaway for wealthy New Yorkers.

beats.script_body: Hangings, protests, burials, parades — if another spot in New York has seen as much drama as Washington Square Park, the guidebook hadn't heard of it. North of the first Dutch settlement in Manhattan, this was originally marshland fed by a stream that still runs under nearby Minetta Lane. Its first settlers were Nieuw Amsterdam slaves who, in 1641, were given partial freedom in return for farming this then-dangerous, remote acreage. They were primarily older men and women who had outlived their usefulness to their masters, and their freedom was a mixed blessing: they had to hand over a large part of their harvests to the colony and, more disturbingly, they became human watchdogs, posted here to alert the Dutch if local Indians or British forces tried to attack.

beats.source_passage: Hangings, protests, burials, parades . . . if there's another spot in New York that's seen as much drama as Washington Square Park has, I've yet to hear of it. Located north of the first Dutch settlement in Manhattan, the area was originally a marshland, fed by the stream that still runs under nearby Minetta Lane (see stop 10, below). Its first settlers were Nieuw Amsterdam slaves who in 1641 were given partial freedom in return for farming this then-dangerous and remote acreage. For these slaves (primarily older men and women who'd outlived their usefulness to their masters), their freedom was a mixed blessing: They had to hand over a large part of their harvests to the colony, and, perhaps more disturbingly, they became human watchdogs, set here to alert the Dutch should local Indians or British forces try to attack.

beats.script_body: In 1797 the drained swamp was designated a potter's field, and it was put to grim use a year later when yellow fever swept the city. Over five percent of New York's population died that muggy, mosquito-infested summer, and the poorest of them — nearly 20,000 people — were buried right here. In 1826 the ground became a military parade ground, and tales were told of soldiers drilling here, their boots slipping through the crust of the dirt and crunching down on shroud-covered skeletons. As if that weren't haunting enough, the square was often used for public hangings, the condemned strung up on a massive elm that still stands on the park's northwest corner.

beats.source_passage: In 1797, the drained swamp was designated a potter's field; it was put to good use a year later when yellow fever swept through what was by then New York City. Over 5% of the population of the city died that muggy, mosquito-infested summer, the poorest of whom were buried here, nearly 20,000 of them. In 1826 it became a military parade ground; tales were told of soldiers doing their drills, boots slipping through the crust of the dirt and crunching down on shroud-covered skeletons. If all this weren't haunting enough, the square was often used for public hangings, the condemned strung up on a massive elm tree that still stands on the park's northwest corner.

beats.script_body: The magnificent white marble arch at the foot of Fifth Avenue was designed by Stanford White — his second such arch. The first, made of wood and plaster, was erected in 1889 to mark the centennial of George Washington's inauguration and to raise funds for this permanent version, completed in 1892. Look to the right side of the arch: the sculpture there, Washington as President, Accompanied by Wisdom and Justice, was added in 1918 by Alexander Stirling Calder, father of the great modern mobile-maker Alexander Calder. On the other side, Washington as Commander-in-Chief, Accompanied by Fame and Valor, by Herman Atkins MacNeill, was tacked on the same year.

beats.source_passage: The magnificent white marble arch at the foot of Fifth Avenue was designed by Stanford White, the second such arch he created (the first, made of wood and plaster, was erected in 1889 to mark the centennial of George Washington's inauguration and to raise funds for this permanent arch, completed in 1892). The sculpture on the right side of the arch, depicting Washington as President, Accompanied by Wisdom and Justice, was added in 1918 by Alexander Stirling Calder, father of the great modern artist and mobile-maker Alexander Calder. On the other side, we see Washington as Commander-in-Chief, Accompanied by Fame and Valor by Herman Atkins MacNeill, also tacked on in 1918.

beats.script_body: The arch has long been a choice target for protesters. In 1918, by Frommer's account, Dada daddy Marcel Duchamp climbed the 110 interior steps with fellow members of the Liberal Club — including a woman who called herself "Woe," so she could declaim "Woe is Me!" — carrying Chinese lanterns, food, wine, and cap guns, to declare Greenwich Village an "independent republic." An unamused constable soon brought them down. Less lighthearted was a 1968 takeover by the Students Against Racism and War, who barricaded themselves inside to hang a banner protesting the Vietnam War. The door to the inner stairway has been bolted ever since.

beats.script_body: In 2020 and 2021 the park became an illegal — and very raucous — after-hours dance party for Covid-weary young people from all corners of the city. Clashes between revelers and noise-weary residents eventually led police to enforce a 10pm curfew in the park. That curfew has since been lifted.

beats.script_body: Dash-dot-dot-dash — you've reached the birthplace of the telegraph. Inventor Samuel Morse lived in this New York University building, where he was a painting instructor, when in 1836 he worked out the rudiments of the telegraphic alphabet better known as Morse Code. A year later, on September 2, 1837, he gathered 1,700 feet of copper wire, coiled it around his room, and sent the world's first wire dispatch from one end to the other.

beats.script_body: You're looking at the longest unbroken string of Greek Revival town houses anywhere in the United States. New York University owns most of them now — in fact it owns much of the neighborhood — but in the 1830s, when they were built, they were strictly for individual owners of the highest social class. The Greek Revival style was no accident. In the mid-1820s, support for the Greeks — a Christian nation fighting for independence from the Ottoman Empire — was all the rage among the upper echelons of Manhattan society. That enthusiasm, plus the notion that America was a modern version of ancient Greek democracy, is why classical columns started popping up on buildings all over town, with Greek symbols worked into fences, pedestals added to facades, and so on.

beats.source_passage: You're now looking at the longest unbroken string of Greek Revival town houses anywhere in the United States. Aren't they lovely? New York University owns most of these (in fact, they own much of the neighborhood), but in the 1830s, when these were built, they were strictly for individual owners of the highest social class. Henry James' grandmother lived here, and he used the area as inspiration for the famed novel Washington Square (later turned into the play and film The Heiress). The use of Greek Revival architecture was no accident. In the mid-1820s, support for the Greeks—a Christian nation fighting for independence from the "heathen" (their term) Ottoman Empire—was all the rage among the upper echelons of Manhattan society. It's one reason (along with the notion that America was a modern version of ancient Greek democracy) why classical columns started popping up on buildings all over town, with Greek symbols incorporated into fences (as you'll see in front of you), pedestals added to facades, and so on.

beats.script_body: On March 25, 1911, a horrific tragedy on this site reshaped New York State law and the history of the American labor movement. That Saturday, some 600 young women — mostly Jewish and Italian immigrants between 13 and 23 — were at work in a garment factory on the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors. At 5pm, just as they were getting ready to leave, a fire sprang up in the southeast corner of the eighth floor; no one has ever determined the cause. Within minutes all three floors were an inferno, and an inescapable one, because many doors had been locked from the outside — to prevent theft, the owners later said. A fire escape collapsed and the elevator operator fled, but a pedestrian named Joseph Zito ran in, got the elevator working, and made five trips up through the flames, saving 25 to 30 workers each time. Still, several young women jumped to their deaths in front of horrified passersby, others suffocated, and some were crushed at the locked doors. In all, 146 people were killed at the Triangle Shirt Waist Factory, most in the first ten minutes of the hour-long blaze.

beats.source_passage: On March 25, 1911, a horrific tragedy on this site reshaped the laws of New York State and the history of the American labor movement. On that Saturday, some 600 young women, mostly Jewish and Italian immigrants between the ages of 13 and 23, were hard at work in a garment factory on the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors of this building. At 5pm, just as the workers were getting ready to leave, a fire sprung up in the southeast corner of the eighth floor—no one has ever been able to determine the cause—and within minutes all three floors were an inferno. An inescapable one, it turned out, because many of the doors had been locked from the outside (to prevent theft, the owners said later). Minutes after that, one of the fire escapes collapsed, and the elevator operator fled in terror. A brave pedestrian named Joseph Zito ran into the building, got the elevator working, and made five trips up through the flames, saving 25 to 30 workers on each trip. Fleeing the flames, several young women jumped to their deaths in front of horrified passersby. Those trapped inside suffocated from the smoke, while still others were crushed in a heap at the locked doors. In all, 146 people were killed at the Triangle Shirt Waist Factory, most within the first 10 minutes of the hour-long blaze.

beats.script_body: The more theatrical strain of Greenwich Village bohemianism found its home at the little theater that once stood here — only the name remains — at one point one of the city's most influential playhouses. That was thanks largely to Eugene O'Neill, who managed it and whose important early works were first performed here, among them Emperor Jones, The Hairy Ape, and The Great God Brown. Overturning barriers, the theater cast African Americans to play African Americans, and even featured a kiss between a Black man and a white woman — a radical move in 1926, one that drew threats from the Ku Klux Klan.

beats.script_body: There are few better Village streets for a quick snack than MacDougal. For a pastry and some java, head to Caffe Reggio. Founded in 1927, it claims to have introduced cappuccino to America, and it has the huge copper machines to prove it — and it has turned up in films like Godfather II and Inside Llewyn Davis. For something more substantial, MacDougal also serves up some of the city's best pita sandwiches at Mamoun's Falafel.

beats.script_body: Listen carefully: a stream still runs below this street, and on a rare quiet day you can hear it gurgling faintly beneath your feet. beats.script_body: In 1863, when the riots surrounding the Civil War's first draft lottery morphed into race riots, this was one of the few safe places in the city for Black Americans. For five days hundreds of white hooligans raged through the streets, beating and lynching Blacks and even burning down an orphanage for Black children — the most violent riot of the century, with 105 people killed and many more maimed for life. But the narrow layout of Minetta Street let armed residents successfully guard their homes and families from harm.

beats.script_body: Attention Hamilton fans: in the 1790s the widowed Aaron Burr moved into this 1767 carriage house with his daughter Theodosia. After the tragic duel, Burr lost not only his political career but much of his property, including this building. It later became an engine house for the local firehouse, and in the 1890s a saloon and brothel. The restaurant here today is still a stop on ghost tours — many claim it's haunted by Aaron, Theodosia, and some of the ladies of the night who once worked here. The specters get blamed whenever a customer's earring goes missing.

beats.script_body: Oddly enough, it was an organized-crime sting operation that precipitated the raid that gave birth to the contemporary gay rights movement. By the 1960s the Genovese crime family owned most gay bars in the Village, serving watered-down liquor to a community that had few other places to meet — and blackmailing wealthier customers with the threat of outing. The family usually paid off the police, but on June 28, 1969, the Stonewall wasn't tipped off. When eight officers showed up at 1:20am and began loading employees and customers into a police van, patrons started pelting them with pennies, cans, bottles, and bricks. The melee escalated, and thousands rioted for another five days before order was restored. While these protests weren't the start of the gay rights movement, many feel they were its galvanizing force — which is why pride celebrations in New York and worldwide now fall on the anniversary weekend of the riots.

Five days of rioting galvanized the gay rights movement; pride falls on the anniversary
beats.source_passage: Oddly enough, it was an organized-crime sting operation that precipitated the raid that gave birth to the contemporary gay rights movement. By the 1960s, the Genovese crime family owned most gay bars in the Village, where they served watered-down liquor to a community that didn't have many other places to meet; they also blackmailed wealthier customers with the threat of outing. The family regularly paid off the police, but on June 28, 1969, the Stonewall wasn't tipped off in advance. When eight police officers showed up at 1:20am and started loading employees and customers into a police van, patrons began pelting them with pennies, cans, bottles, and bricks. As the melee escalated, thousands of people rioted for another 5 days before order could be restored. While these protests weren't the start of the gay rights movement, many feel that they were the galvanizing force. Today, pride celebrations in New York, and worldwide, take place on the anniversary weekend of the riots.

fact_check.notes: June 28, 1969 date, 1:20am raid, and organized-crime/Genovese ownership corroborated by Wikipedia, Britannica, History.com.
